Chapter 7: Shrinking Delay—Making Rewards Immediate and Progress Visible.
Delay is a sneaky thief when it comes to motivation, isn’t it? When the reward for your hard work feels far off, it’s just so much easier to lose momentum. Our minds are naturally pulled toward rewards that we can see and touch right now. So, if the payoff feels distant, staying motivated gets tough.
But what if you could pull those rewards closer? What if progress wasn’t just something you felt at the end, but something you could see and celebrate along the way?
One of the best ways to do this is by breaking big, far-off goals into smaller, bite-sized milestones. Every time you hit one of these mini-goals, you get a burst of accomplishment and a renewed sense of momentum. Imagine you’re working on a big project. Instead of worrying about the whole thing, just aim to finish one section today—and give yourself a little celebration for every small win.
There are other great tricks for shrinking delay, too.
Try building in immediate rewards. For instance, pair that not-so-exciting task with something you enjoy—like listening to your favorite podcast while you organize files, or promising yourself a walk after a focused work session. Suddenly, the task feels lighter, and the reward is right there waiting for you.
Another smart move? Make your progress visible. Use checklists, charts, or even a simple progress bar. Every time you check something off or move it from “to-do” to “done”, you get that satisfying rush that comes from seeing real progress.
And don’t forget the power of feedback loops. Share your progress with a friend, a mentor, or a group. Sometimes, just having someone cheer you on—or even just knowing you’ll share an update—makes the journey feel more immediate and rewarding.
Picture someone training for a marathon. The race itself might be months away, but by logging each daily run, celebrating those weekly improvements, and sharing milestones with a running group, they turn a single, distant finish line into a string of near-term victories.
Here’s the key takeaway: the journey to your goal should feel rewarding in the present, not just at the end. When you shrink the gap between effort and payoff, motivation sticks around, and procrastination loses its grip.
